list.listitem: Combinations of symptoms in a clinical decision rule are useful to guide testing and antibiotic use in patients with pharyngitis. A

A rapid detection antigen test (RADT) can be used to rule out strep throat in patients with intermediate probability of strep pharyngitis. Backup throat culture after negative RADT is not necessary especially in settings with low rheumatic fever incidence. A

The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) recommends RADT for all patients with pharyngitis except for children under age 3 years or when sore throat is accompanied by overt viral features like rhinorrhea, cough, oral ulcers, and hoarseness. C

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American College of Physicians (ACP, 2016) recommend testing adult patients with symptoms suggestive of group A streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis with RADT or culture and treating with antibiotics only those testing positive. A
Penicillin is the drug of choice for adults, while amoxicillin or penicillin is usually prescribed for children. A
Acetaminophen is recommended for throat pain; aspirin should be avoided in children due to the risk of Reye's syndrome. B
A single dose of a corticosteroid (oral or intramuscular) can be considered to improve pain at 24 to 48 hours. B

background.definition: Inflammation of the pharyngeal mucosa; pharynx refers to the part of the alimentary canal from the mouth cavity to the esophagus. This chapter focuses primarily on infectious causes in adults. Pharyngitis in children is addressed in another chapter.

list.listitem: Based on data from the 1989-1999 National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NAMCS), there were an estimated 6.7 million annual visits by adults for sore throat.
In the 2014 NAMCS, there were 7.72 million visits to community health centers by patients of all ages for sore throats.

Based on nationally representative surveys of outpatient care provision and insurance claims data, authors of one review estimated that GAS pharyngitis caused 19.1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 17.3-21.1) outpatient visits and 10.2 (95% CI 9.0-11.5) antibiotic prescriptions per 1000 US persons aged 0 to 64 years, annually.
The CDC states that GAS is responsible for about 5% to 15% of pharyngitis infections in adults and 20% to 30% of pharyngitis episodes in children.
In one study, of 809 adult patients undergoing tracheal intubation for elective surgical procedures, 44% of women and 33% of men reported postoperative sore throat.

Based on the average number of primary healthcare episodes managed annually in New Zealand general practices (2014-2016) and on the average number of hospitalizations occurring each year (2005-2014), GAS affects 1.5% of the population, resulting in an annual economic burden of 29.2 million NZ dollars (2015 prices) and a health burden of 2373 disability-adjusted life years.
Pharyngitis is the 18th most common diagnosis in ambulatory care.
In the US in 1999 to 2000, there were 11.29 million ambulatory care visits for acute pharyngitis; 68.6% of the visits were to primary care offices.

In a systematic review of 18 studies from 12 countries across 5 continents with a median of 250,00 patients per study, pharyngitis was the 4th most common reason for visits to a primary-care clinician.
In a cohort study of 14,610 adults with acute sore throat, 1.3% of participants developed complications overall and 14.2% re-consulted with new or unresolved symptoms.
Pharyngitis can be caused by infectious agents, acid reflux,postnasal drip (including allergic), persistent cough, or trauma from intubation.
Infectious causes can be viral (including Epstein-Barr virus [EBV] and cytomegalovirus [CMV]), bacterial (eg, GABHS, chlamydia, mycoplasma), or fungal; viral are most common.
Only 5% to 15% of adult cases of acute pharyngitis are caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GABHS). Rates of GABHS are higher for children (24.6%-42%).
Among 1556 patients hospitalized with coronavirus (COVID)-19 from 5 retrospective studies, sore throat was present in 12.4%.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies of patients with sore throat found prevalence rates of Group C streptococcus of 6.1% (95% CI 3.2%-9.0%) and Fusobacterium necrophorum of 18.9% (95% CI 10.5%-27.2%). It is not clear if these bacteria are pathogenic.
Risk factors for GABHS are listed below.
Infectious agents cause an inflammatory response in the pharyngeal mucosa resulting in pain.

With respect to GAS pharyngitis, infection vs. colonization is likely due to a complex interaction of bacterial virulence and host genetics and immunocompetence. One group of investigators suggest a role for bacterial superantigens activating the immune system and resulting in acute rheumatic fever.
Stomach acid causes sore throat from direct irritation.
Allergy or sinusitis causes sore throat from both direct irritation and drying.

Postoperative sore throat can be reduced by the following interventions: use of a laryngeal mask airway vs. endotracheal tube during surgery; use of a tapered-cuff endotracheal tube; EMLA (eutectic mixture of local anesthetics) cream over the endotracheal tube cuff; perioperative intravenous lidocaine or corticosteriods; and topical magnesium, licorice or steroids. B

Although no commercial vaccine is available against GAS, investigation into a vaccine is ongoing and would likely reduce the burden and cost of disease significantly. Authors of one study estimated that a 30-valent GAS vaccine with 80% efficacy could prevent 5.4% (95% CI 4.6%-6.4%) of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions among children aged 3 to 9 years.

Use of a laryngeal mask airway vs. endotracheal tube during surgery reduces the incidence and severity of sore throat. In one RCT, using an insertion technique for a laryngeal mask airway of leaving the blocker attached to the end of the pilot balloon resulted in a reduced incidence (16.2% vs. 31.9% in the blocker removal group) and severity of postoperative sore throat.

In an RCT of 191 adults, intubation using an endotracheal tube with a tapered cuff reduced the incidence (32% vs. 54%) and severity of postoperative sore throat and incidence of hoarseness (19% vs. 37%).

In another RCT, the addition of lidocaine to the distal part of a tapered endotracheal tube actually increased the incidence of post-operative sore throat. However, use of EMLA cream over the endotracheal tube cuff reduced the incidence and severity of postoperative sore throat at up to 2 hours and the proportion of patients with significant postoperative sore throat over 24 hours (9.8% vs 43.1% in the placebo arm) in an RCT including 204 adult patients.

Intravenous (IV) lidocaine administered during the perioperative period reduces the incidence of postoperative sore throat (risk ratio [RR] 0.46; 95% CI 0.32-0.67) as well as post-extubation cough (RR 0.64; 95% CI 0.48-0.86), based on a systematic review of 16 trials. Authors of a second meta-analysis of trials on lidocaine confirmed benefit of IV and intra-cuff lidocaine on post-operative sore throat but no benefit from lidocaine jelly or spray.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies with 400 patients found perioperative IV dexmedetomidine reduced the incidence of post-operative sore throat (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.40-0.77), but also increased risk of bradycardia (RR: 2.46; 95% CI 1.28-4.71) and hypotension (RR 3.26; 95% CI 1.14-9.33).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 70 RCTs with 7141 patients concluded that topical application of magnesium (OR 0.10; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.03-0.26), licorice (OR 0.14; 95% CrI 0.03-0.55), or steroids (OR 0.11; 95% CrI 0.06-0.22) were most effective in preventing postoperative sore throat at 24 hours and more effective than topical lidocaine.

Remifentanil, a short-acting synthetic opioid, is sometimes given to patients undergoing general anesthesia to prevent post-operative sore throat. In one RCT of 92 patients, those randomized to high-dose remifentanil had a higher incidence of post-operative sore throat than those receiving the lower dose of 0.05 μg/kg/min; overall incidence was 72% vs. 39%, respectively.

Acupuncture point stimulation vs. no or sham stimulation was associated with a reduced incidence (risk ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.18-0.55) and decreased severity (standardized mean difference -2.79, 95% CI -4.59 to - 0.99) of post-operative sore throat based on a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs and 1 comparative study.
Rigors, cough, and epidemic make influenza more likely. Tonsillar exudates and enlargement, adenopathy, and absence of cough make GABHS more likely. C
Combinations of symptoms can be useful for predicting strep throat using a clinical prediction rule. A

A rapid detection antigen test (RADT) can be used to rule out strep throat in patients with intermediate probability of strep pharyngitis. Backup throat culture after negative RADT is not necessary especially in settings with low rheumatic fever incidence. A

The IDSA (2012) recommends RADT for all patients with pharyngitis except for children under age 3 years or when sore throat is accompanied by overt viral features like rhinorrhea, cough, oral ulcers, and hoarseness. C

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2023) and American College of Physicians (ACP, 2016) recommend testing adult patients with symptoms suggestive of GAS pharyngitis with RADT or culture and treating with antibiotics only those testing positive. A

Remote assessment of strep throat in virtual visits suggests that patients/parents/caregivers were very g may be very gg out pus and inflammation, but overcalling resulted in lower specificity, and photographs were of sufficient quality for clinical assessment less than half the time. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Fatigue, nausea and anorexia without vomiting, symmetric lymphadenopathy, teenaged or young adult, hepatosplenomegaly
Oropharyngeal vesicles and ulcers, vesicles on hands and feet
Asymmetry of neck, displacement of pharyngeal wall or uvula, "hot potato voice," toxic appearance
Rapid onset of fever, malaise, sore throat, drooling, absence of cough
Sore throat, low-grade fever, malaise, pharyngeal erythema with gray pseudomembrane
Fever, tonsillar exudate and enlargement, adenopathy, and no cough are typical
Typical reflux symptoms (ie, water brash, belching, epigastric pain, and association with meals)

Differential.Differential_Name: Postnasal drip due to allergies or sinus infection
Differential.Differential_Features: Fever unlikely with allergies; sinusitis usually causes facial pain

list.listitem: The typical patient with pharyngitis reports sore throat. Additional findings can include cough, fever, myalgia, palatal petechiae, tonsillar enlargement, and exudates. A history of exposure increases suspicion of strep. However, physicians cannot differentiate bacterial from viral respiratory tract infections based on their clinical impression.

Authors of a systematic review of outpatient diagnostic accuracy studies found a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of 2.1, 95% CI 1.6-2.8 and negative LR (LR-) of 0.47, 95% 0.36-0.60 for clinical impression (gestalt) for streptococcal pharyngitis in adults and children.
The symptom most strongly associated with influenza is rigors (LR+ 8).
The presence of sore throat makes coronavirus-19 less likely than having a different infectious disease (positive likelihood ratio 0.814, 95% CI 0.714 to 0.929).
Fatigue is more common in infectious mononucleosis.

Patients with GAS pharyngitis may report sudden onset of sore throat, exudative tonsillitis, tender anterior cervical nodes, history of fever, headache, and abdominal pain without cough, rhinorrhea, or hoarseness. Signs and symptoms most strongly associated with GABHS pharyngitis are strep exposure and tonsillar exudates but the of individual findings are weak.

Combinations of symptoms, however, can be useful for predicting strep throat (see Clinical Decision Rules section). For example, in a meta-analysis, the Centor score had reasonable specificity (82%) and a post-test probability of 12% to 40% based on a prior prevalence of 5% to 20% (ie, the test is less useful in low prevalence populations).

Combining the Centor score with real-time local incidence data (for the past 14 days) for GAS could reduce missed cases and reduce antibiotic use; however, these data are not readily available and the approach has not been tested in clinical practice.

In a study of virtual care including 33 adults and 12 children with sore throat, most were able to provide enough information on clinical features to calculate a FeverPAIN score (76% of adults and 83% for children), but less than half were able to provide photographs of sufficient quality for assessment (39% of adults 42% of children). Using clinician assessment as reference standard, self/parent/carer assessment of inflammation had a sensitivity of 100%, specificity of 46.7%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 27.3% and negative predictive value (NPV) of 100%. For assessment of pus, the sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV were 76.5%, 100%, 71.4%, 42.9% and 100%. This makes self-assessment potentially helpful for ruling out strep throat.
Clinical history, physical examination, and scores to predict bacterial infection were not useful for identifying those who develop suppurative complications.

There are three major types of RADTs - latex agglutination, enzyme immunoassay, and optical immunoassay. These are performed using a posterior pharyngeal swab specimen. The tests work by acid extraction, used to solubilize GAS cell wall carbohydrate, followed by an immunologic reaction which detects the presence or absence of the Lancefield group A carbohydrate, a GAS-specific cell-wall antigen. Advantages are ease of use, low cost and quick results (<10 minutes).
RADT can be used to rule out strep throat in patients with suspected GAS pharyngitis. Rapid antigen tests based on optical immunoassays or DNA probe technology have a sensitivity approaching 90%.

Authors of a systematic review of 48 studies worldwide reported sensitivity of RADTs of 86% (95% CI 83%-88%) and specificity of 96% (94%-97%). Using these numbers and a prevalence rate of 10%, of 100 individuals with strep throat, 86 would be correctly detected with the rapid test while 13 would be missed and not receive antibiotic treatment.

These numbers were confirmed in a Cochrane review of RADT in children (sensitivity 85.6% and specificity 95.4%). The authors concluded, based on these results, that of 100 children with strep throat, 86 would be correctly detected with the rapid test while 14 would be missed and not receive antibiotic treatment.

The IDSA (2012) recommends RADT for all patients with pharyngitis except for children under age 3 years or when sore throat is accompanied by overt viral features like rhinorrhea, cough, oral ulcers, and hoarseness. CDC/ACP support testing using RADT or culture in adult patients with symptoms suggestive of group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

NAATs are also available for diagnosing GAS. The test works by amplifying (making many copies) of the bacteria or virus genetic material present in a specimen. Probe testing detects nucleic acid sequences specific to GAS. These tests are higher cost, and most studies have been conducted in laboratory settings.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 38 studies found a summary sensitivity of 97.5% (95% CI 96.2%-98.3%) and summary specificity of 95.1% (95% CI 93.6%-96.3%). The NAAT tests were more sensitive than RADTs (13 studies; 96.8% versus 82.3%) with no difference in specificity.
Throat culture is not considered necessary for adults with a negative RADT due to the low likelihood that it will change management.
In one retrospective study, the use of throat swabs for patients with sore throat did not influence antimicrobial treatment; 24% of 247 patients had a positive culture result.
Nasopharyngeal swab was better than either nasal wash or oropharyngeal swab for virus detection in adults with acute pharyngitis.

In a study of 101 consecutive adults and 99 children with sore throat and a Centor score >2, sensitivity of mouth culture was 72.1% (95% CI 59.9%-82.3%) and specificity was 100% (95% CI 92.7%-89.4%-100%) using throat culture as the reference standard.

If RADT is not available, a throat culture can be obtained for patients with moderate probability of strep; antibiotics are started for patients with positive cultures (treatment within 1 week of onset is likely to prevent rheumatic fever).
Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis is discussed in more detail in that chapter.

The modified Centor/McIsaac clinical prediction rule assigning 1 point each to fever, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, tonsillar exudates, and age less than 15 increases the probability of strep from 1% with no points to 51% with 4 to 5 points.Using this rule would potentially reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions by 64%.

The Centor rule was prospectively validated in a sample of more than 200,000 children and adults presenting to urgent care clinics with sore throat. In this study, among patients 15 years or older (of whom 23% tested positive for GABHS), 7% of those with a Centor score of 0; 12% of those with a Centor score of 1; 21% of those with a Centor score of 2; 38% of those with a Centor score of 3; and 57% of those with a Centor score of 4 tested positive (95% CI were within 2%). For patients aged 3 years or older (of whom 27% tested positive for GABHS), nearly identical rates of testing positive were found—8% of those with a McIsaac score of 0 up to 55% of those with a McIsaac score of 4 tested positive for GABHS.

Another score for predicting a viral sore throat, called the Mistik score, includes the following variables: absence of headache, stuffy nose, sneezing, temperature of ≥37.5°C on physical examination, and absence of tonsillar exudate and/or swelling. The probability of a viral pharyngitis in those with a score of 5 was 82.1% in a population of 624 patients (of whom viral infection was found in 44.3% and GABHS infection in 18.5%). The score remains to be validated.

In a randomized clinical trial (RCT), clinicians randomized to having access to two clinical decision-support tools—the Walsh rule for streptococcal pharyngitis and the Heckerling rule for pneumonia—reduced their rate of antibiotic prescribing by 9.2%. The intervention group completed the prediction rule tool in just over half of visits.

In another RCT, patients randomized to antibiotic use based on either a clinical score alone or RADT based on a clinical score had similar rates of improved symptoms and reduced antibiotic use compared with delayed antibiotic prescribing.

However, in an RCT of 541 providers from 33 practices with 100,573 patient visits, use of an integrated clinical prediction rule system designed to determine the risk of bacterial infection from reason for visit of sore throat, cough, or upper respiratory infection and guide evidence-based evaluation and treatment, there was no difference in antibiotic prescribing or orders for RADTs between intervention and control groups. In this trial, however, intervention providers only completed the tool in 6.9% of eligible visits.

Interestingly, in a study comparing published guidelines for sore throat, most of the 6 high-quality guidelines no longer recommended the systematic use of diagnostic scores and tests or antibiotic therapy to prevent acute rheumatic fever or loco-regional complications, except for high-risk patients.
Use a clinical rule to establish the risk of GABHS for adults; usefulness is less clear for children. Suspect influenza during an epidemic in patients with fever and cough.

For patients with an intermediate probability of strep, RADT can be used; a negative test will miss about 5% of patients with GABHS. An alternative is to use RADT for all patients, especially for children between ages 3 and 14 years.

A throat culture is recommended by some guidelines for children with a negative RADT. Newer optical immunoassay tests are more accurate and may preclude the need for follow-up culture. The role of NAAT is not yet clear.
Antibiotics for sore throat shorten symptom duration by about 1 day and prevent suppurative (otitis media, sinusitis, and peritonsillar abscess) and nonsuppurative (rheumatic fever) complications. A

Penicillin (250-500 mg twice daily for 10 days) is the drug of choice for adults. Penicillin or amoxicillin is usually prescribed for children. Shorter courses (≤ 5 days) of antibiotics may be as effective as longer courses (≥10 days). A

For symptomatic relief of throat pain, acetaminophen (1 g every 6 hours [adult] or 15-20 mg/kg every 6 hours [child]) is the drug of choice. Aspirin for throat pain should be avoided in children due to the risk of Reye's syndrome.B
Corticosteroids (single dose of oral or intramuscular) can also be useful to improve pain resolution (NNT ~4-9 to prevent one person continuing to experience pain at 24-48 hours).B

Antibiotics for sore throat shorten symptom duration by about 1 day and prevent suppurative (otitis media, sinusitis, and peritonsillar abscess) and nonsuppurative (rheumatic fever) complications. The number needed to treat to prevent one sore throat at day 3 was less than 6.

If deciding in favor of antibiotic use for sore throat, a strategy of immediate use was only modestly more effective than delayed use for relieving fever and, maybe, pain. There appears to be no difference in clinical outcomes between strategy of delayed antibiotics and no antibiotics.Initiation of treatment within 48 hours may provide the best chance for symptom relief.
The European Society for Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases guideline does not support use of antibiotics for prevention of suppurative complications in sore throat.

Data on prevention of rheumatic fever are largely based on longitudinal studies; a meta-analysis of 10 older trials (1950-1961) with mostly poor methodology found a protective effect of antibiotics against rheumatic fever (RR, 0.32; 95% CI 0.21-0.48) with a NNT of 53. Because the incidence of rheumatic fever is about 60 times lower than in 1960, the NNT is estimated at 3000 to 4000.
Antibiotic use, however, may reduce the rate of transmission (which is 35%), as communicability is reduced to 24 hours.
Penicillin (250-500 mg twice daily for 10 days) is the drug of choice for adults; the IDSA also lists amoxicillin (20-40 mg/kg/d divided 3 times daily for 10 days) as a first-line choice.

In an RCT of 433 patients aged 6 years and older with GAS pharyngitis, penicillin V 800 mg four times daily for five days was non-inferior to penicillin V 1000 mg three times daily for 10 days with respect to clinical outcome, number of relapses (8 and 7 patients, respectively), and complications (0 and 4 patients, respectively) at 3-month follow-up. Side effects were more frequent and of longer duration with 10-day treatment.

Alternative antibiotics for adults include cephalosporin (15-50 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 10 days), erythromycin ethylsuccinate (40 mg/kg/d 2-4 times daily for 10 days), and clindamycin. Authors of a Cochrane review examining different antibiotic choices were uncertain if there were clinically relevant differences between antibiotics for GABHS, although cephalosporins could be considered first-line in adults with relapse (NNT to benefit 50).
A single dose of corticosteroids (oral or IM) can be considered to reduce throat pain at 24-48 hours and is recommended by one expert panel, based on weak evidence (NNT = 5-9; 95% CI 4-59).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 trials found that corticosteroids reduced the time to clinically meaningful pain relief (WMD −4.54 hours; 95% CI −7.19 to −1.89) especially for patients with GABHS pharyngitis; however, they provided only a small reduction in pain scores at 24 hours (WMD −0.90 on a 0-10 visual analog scale; 95% CI −1.5 to −0.3).

Authors of another meta-analysis of 10 trials with 1426 patients with sore throat confirmed that patients receiving a single low dose of corticosteroids were twice as likely to experience pain relief after 24 hours (RR 2.2; 95% CI 1.2-4.3) and 1.5 times more likely to have no pain at 48 hours (RR, 1.5; 95% CI 1.3-1.8). Rates of adverse events were similar between groups.

In the most recent RCT of 565 adults with acute sore throat but non-severe throat pain, a single dose of 10 mg of oral dexamethasone did not increase the proportion of patients with symptom resolution at 24 hours, but increased the proportion of patient reporting complete symptom resolution at 48 hours regardless of antibiotic prescribing (35.4% vs. 27.1% in the placebo group; NNT = 12; 95% CI 7-146). The effect was modest, and given the lack of other benefits the authors conclude that their use is not warranted.

Authors of a Cochrane review of eight trials found reduced mean time to onset of pain relief with corticosteroids by 6 hours and mean time to complete resolution of pain by 14 hours. NNT was <4 to prevent one person continuing to experience pain at 24 hours. This was a heterogeneous group of trials, including patients with both severe and mild/moderate throat pain. The IDSA does not recommend use of corticosteroids as adjunctive treatment.

Acetaminophen (1 g every 6 hours [adult]) is the drug of choice. Ibuprofen (200-600 mg every 8 hours) can be used as an alternative unless the patient has a history of peptic ulcer disease, is eating poorly, has aspirin sensitivity, or renal dysfunction.
Twenty-five mg ibuprofen throat lozenges were more effective than placebo in reducing sore throat pain for up to 24 hours based on a RCT of 385 adults.
There are limited data for determining the effectiveness of tonsillectomy for adults or children with chronic/recurrent acute tonsillitis.
Evidence supporting surgery is of low quality from 2 small trials with inadequate follow-up for adults and insufficient for drawing conclusions.

In an RCT of 268 patients using sore throat diaries and a quality-of-life measure, tonsillectomy vs. medical therapy reduced the number of sore throats by 3.5 in 2 years. Further, in a systematic review of eight trials, tonsillectomy improved overall quality of life in adults with chronic or recurrent tonsillitis. Rates of severe pharyngitis were similar.

Tonsillectomy for recurrent sore throat vs. standard non-surgical care resulted in fewer days of sore throat during 24 months (incident rate ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.65) in a recent RCT performed in the UK. In this study, 453 eligible participants, of 4165 screened, aged 16 and older who were newly referred to secondary care otolaryngology clinics with recurrent acute tonsillitis were randomized to elective tonsillectomy within 8 weeks after random assignment vs. standard non-surgical care for 24 months. Adverse events related to the tonsillectomy were reported in 90 (39%) of 231 participants; the most common adverse effect was bleeding.

There are insufficient data to show one method of tonsillectomy to be superior to another. Authors of a Turkish RCT with 144 patients found tonsillectomy with harmonic scalpel was associated with lower postoperative pain scores than bipolar diathermy tonsillectomy.
There is no evidence that use of a perioperative local anesthetic improves postoperative pain control.
Herbal tea containing demulcents may be effective for short term (<30 min) pain relief.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend zinc gluconate. However, in a RCT of 79 patients undergoing low- or moderate-risk surgery with endotracheal intubation, administration of a single dose of 40-mg zinc lozenge 30 minutes preoperatively effectively reduced both immediate severity and incidence of post-operative sore throat.
There are insufficient high-quality trials to recommend Chinese medicinal herbs for sore throat relief.

Kikyo-to, a combination of glycyrrhiza root and platycodon root extracts used in Japan for relieving sore throat accompanying an upper respiratory tract infection was no more effective than placebo in pain relief at 10 minutes in an RCT of 70 patients.
Authors of a systematic review found a single negative trial demonstrating no benefit from the use of the probiotic Streptococcus salivarius K12 for adults with acute pharyngitis.

However, in a RCT including 70 children aged 6 months to 5 years with acute respiratory illness, a probiotic product containing L. reuteri ATCC PTA 5289 and L. reuteri DSM 17938 vs. placebo ingested orally for 10 days as adjuvants to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs resulted in a lower severity of sore throat beginning on day 3 among those in the intervention group.

In an RCT including 60 adult patients with acute viral pharyngitis, both A. paniculate spray and a positive control chamomile spray were successful in reducing severity of signs and symptoms, but the former had a more rapid treatment response (1.9 ± 0.7 days compared to 2.5 ± 1.2 days, respectively).
Alternatives for pain relief include gargling with warm salt water, eating soft foods, drinking cool or warm beverages, and sucking throat lozenges or popsicles.

Use of benzydamine hydrochloride (a locally-acting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug with local anesthetic and analgesic properties) oromucosal spray or lozenges was effective in reducing sore throat symptoms within 2 minutes and lasting up to 4 hours in adults, based on a European multicenter, randomized, active-controlled, open label study including 363 adult patients with recent onset (≤3 days) of sore throat and a diagnosis of tonsillopharyngitis.
In one RCT with165 patients, benzocaine lozenges were superior to placebo lozenges for reducing pain intensity over 2 hours.
In a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs, a local anesthetic tablet ambroxol at 20 mg resulted in a significant difference in pain reduction vs. placebo mint-flavored lozenge at 3 hours.

A lozenge containing 0.5 mg tyrothricin, 1.0 mg benzalkonium chloride, and 1.5 mg benzocaine was also more effective than placebo with complete resolution of throat pain and swallowing difficulty achieved by 44.6% vs. 27.2% of patients in the control group.

In an RCT of 90 patients with moderate-to-severe pharyngitis symptoms, the sum score for three primary symptoms (pain on swallowing, urge to cough, and hoarseness) decreased by 79.5% in the 35 using ectoine lozenges, 72.2% in the 35 using hyaluronic acid lozenges, and 44.8% for those using saline gargle at 1-week. Ectoine is a compound found in bacteria that acts as an osmolyte protecting against osmotic stress and has moisturizing and anti-inflammatory properties.
In a primary-care RCT of 1009 patients (final results available for 68%), neither probiotics nor chewing xylitol-based gum was effective for reducing severity of symptoms of pharyngitis.
Among adult patients with persistent sore throat, a RCT of 346 patients found no benefit on symptom scores between those randomized to twice daily lansoprazole (a proton pump inhibitor) vs. placebo.
Although 10 days is the traditional treatment duration (primarily to prevent complications), shorter courses of most antibiotics are also effective.

In an RCT of 433 patients aged 6 years and older with GAS pharyngitis, penicillin V 800 mg four times daily for five days was non-inferior to penicillin V 1000 mg three times daily for 10 days with respect to clinical outcome, number of relapses (8 and 7 patients, respectively), and complications (0 and 4 patients, respectively) at 3-month follow-up. Side effects were more frequent and of longer duration with 10-day treatment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 50 RCTs found short-course antibiotic treatment to be as effective as long-course antibiotic treatment for early clinical cure (OR 0.85; 95% CI 0.79-1.15). Subgroup analysis showed equal or greater clinical effectiveness for short- vs. long-course macrolides and cephalosporins, but short-course penicillin was less effective for early clinical cure (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.23-0.82) in comparison to long-course penicillin. More patients assigned to short-course antibiotic therapy experienced overall adverse events (17.7% vs. 12.3%; OR 1.35; 95% CI 1.08-1.68), but long-course penicillin is associated with more moderate adverse events than short-course antibiotics (33% vs 23%, based on 1 trial only).
If symptoms have not improved in 72 hours, the patient should be re-evaluated for an alternative diagnosis or complication (eg, peritonsillar abscess).

Potential complications of strep pharyngitis are otitis media, sinusitis, peritonsillar abscess, and rheumatic fever. Peritonsillar abscess and peritonsillar cellulitis also occur independently from acute tonsillitis and do not show the same seasonal variation.
Peritonsillar abscess can be diagnosed using intraoral ultrasound and is usually effectively managed with steroids and combination penicillin and metronidazole.
Cases of acute rheumatic fever have been decreasing in the US; this is likely due to a decrease in rheumatogenic strains of GABHS (from 49.7% in the 1960s to 10.6% from 2000-2004).

Persistent infection should be treated with antibiotics that cover both group A strep and beta lactamase-producing organisms; options include erythromycin, cephalexin, clindamycin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and IM ceftriaxone.

Authors of a systematic review of five RCTs at high risk of bias concluded that clindamycin and amoxicillin with clavulanate were likely superior to penicillin with respect to microbiological effects and number of future episodes of acute tonsillitis in patients with recurrent acute tonsillitis.
Patients with GAS experience symptom improvement within 48 to 72 hours of initiating antibiotic therapy (a benefit of ~1 day). B
Antibiotics will prevent about 70% of cases of acute rheumatic fever, 84% of subsequent cases of peritonsillar abscess, 75% of cases of otitis media, and half the cases of sinusitis. A

Acute rheumatic fever is a rare complication of GAS pharyngitis estimated to occur in <2 cases per 100,000 school-aged children in the U.S., compared to 150 cases per 100,000 worldwide. Ten percent of cases will result in complications and 1% die. B
An estimated 1% to 2.4% with untreated GAS will develop a peritonsillar abscess. B
